problem_plain: Graphics processors were designed to render pixels, not to run AI models or encrypt data. As AI, cryptography, robotics, and quantum computing each impose unique patterns of computation — some deeply sequential, some massively parallel, some dominated by memory traffic rather than arithmetic — a single chip architecture cannot serve all of them well. The research in this theme asks: when a workload is so different from neural-network training that a GPU is fundamentally the wrong tool, what chip should replace it? The answers span everything from silicon that computes directly on encrypted data, to chips that control quantum processors, to processors printed on flexible plastic that can bend around a wrist.
why_plain: Every specialized domain has a distinct bottleneck that mismatches the GPU's strengths. Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) — computing on data that remains encrypted end-to-end — inflates every number into a polynomial thousands of elements long, so even simple addition floods memory buses rather than stressing arithmetic cores. Quantum processors require nanosecond-precise classical control signals and low-latency feedback; standard server software stacks are too slow by orders of magnitude. Robotics and spatial-mapping algorithms alternate between dense matrix math and highly irregular pointer-chasing, which neither CPUs nor GPUs handle gracefully. The common thread is that each domain's bottleneck is data movement and timing, not raw multiply-accumulate throughput.
approach_plain: Researchers respond by designing chips, compilers, and algorithms that co-evolve together — hardware shaped to eliminate the specific data-movement bottleneck of one domain, paired with a compiler that generates code exploiting the hardware's unique capabilities. Three broad strategies recur: (1) place computation physically next to the data it needs, eliminating the wire between processor and memory; (2) redesign the algorithm so it produces less data in the first place; (3) build reconfigurable or programmable substrate that can reshape itself to the irregular workload pattern rather than forcing the workload into a rigid pipeline.

groups.heading: Chips that compute on encrypted data (Fully Homomorphic Encryption)
groups.explain: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) lets a server compute on data it cannot read — the data stays encrypted the entire time. The catch is that each encrypted number is a polynomial with thousands of coefficients, and routine operations like addition swell into multi-megabyte transfers. The GPU's memory bus saturates long before its arithmetic units are busy. The papers here attack this by moving arithmetic physically into memory (so data never crosses the bus), by distributing computation across many chips, by reformulating algorithms to reduce the number of expensive operations, and by writing compilers that place the unavoidable 'level-reset' operations — bootstrapping, which refreshes the noise budget that builds up each time you multiply two encrypted numbers — in the fewest possible locations.

papers.name: FHENDI
papers.gloss: Puts arithmetic units inside DRAM itself; a conflict-free wiring scheme enables butterfly operations within memory banks, cutting mean latency 2145x vs CPU

papers.name: Anaheim
papers.gloss: Identifies that FHE's true GPU bottleneck is element-wise modular addition (not complex transforms), then moves those ops into DRAM with purpose-built in-memory arithmetic units

papers.name: Cinnamon
papers.gloss: Splits FHE computation across many small chiplets instead of one giant die; co-designed compiler and algorithms reduce inter-chip traffic, achieving BERT inference in 1.67 seconds vs 17 hours on CPU

papers.name: Hydra
papers.gloss: Distributes FHE deep-learning inference across multiple FPGA server cards using model-level pipeline parallelism; 74–160x faster than comparable single-card designs

papers.name: WarpDrive
papers.gloss: First to run GPU tensor cores (matrix-math units) and general CUDA cores simultaneously inside the same FHE transform kernel; 13.4x transform throughput improvement on an A100

papers.name: Neo
papers.gloss: Reformulates FHE polynomial arithmetic as matrix multiplications so GPU tensor cores can accelerate it; makes high-throughput cryptographic hardware available without new silicon

papers.name: EFFACT
papers.gloss: Full-stack FHE platform (compiler + FPGA/ASIC hardware) with a streaming memory scheme that sustains high throughput using small on-chip memory, plus circuit reuse to cut chip area

papers.name: FAST
papers.gloss: FHE accelerator supporting two different key-switching algorithms and adjustable arithmetic precision in one chip, dynamically switching based on how much noise budget (ciphertext level) remains

papers.name: ReSBM
papers.gloss: Compiler that finds the minimum number of bootstrapping (level-reset) operations needed using a graph min-cut algorithm, provably reducing the costliest FHE step

papers.name: HALO
papers.gloss: First compiler to correctly place bootstrapping operations inside program loops, enabling automated FHE compilation of iterative algorithms without programmer intervention

papers.name: CIPHERMATCH
papers.gloss: Redesigns encrypted string search to use only cheap additions (no multiplications), then adds a compute unit inside flash storage to avoid moving ciphertext data to DRAM at all

Three new CPU vector instructions (MQX extension) close the gap between commodity x86 CPUs and cryptographic ASICs for transforms used in FHE and post-quantum cryptography; 38x speedup over prior CPU code

groups.heading: Silicon for zero-knowledge proofs and privacy-preserving verification
groups.explain: A zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) is a mathematical certificate that lets one party convince another it knows a secret — or ran a computation correctly — without revealing the underlying data. Blockchains and verifiable AI use ZKPs constantly, but generating one proof can take minutes on a CPU because it requires huge polynomial multiplications and multi-scalar multiplications (aggregating thousands of elliptic-curve points). These operations share the FHE problem of being memory-traffic-intensive, but their internal structure is different enough to warrant separate hardware.

papers.name: zkSpeed
papers.gloss: Custom ASIC with eight dedicated hardware units for the HyperPlonk ZKP protocol; shared multipliers across proof phases cut chip area 49%; 801x faster than a server CPU

papers.name: LegoZK
papers.gloss: Reconfigurable ASIC where one type of arithmetic unit handles every ZKP phase by changing its internal wiring at runtime; 32x faster than prior ZKP ASIC, 37% lower power

papers.name: UniZK
papers.gloss: Systolic-array (grid of multiply-add cells) extended with extra local connections and a vector mode, letting one unified fabric handle all ZKP kernel types; 97x over CPU, 840x over prior ASICs

papers.name: BatchZK
papers.gloss: GPU pipeline that overlaps successive proof-generation stages across many proofs simultaneously, turning a sequential per-proof flow into a throughput-optimized batch; aimed at blockchain applications
Multi-GPU NTT (number-theoretic transform, a key step in ZKP) that restructures the butterfly computation to minimize data transferred between GPUs, enabling scalable multi-GPU ZKP generation

papers.name: Finesse
papers.gloss: Compiler + ASIC co-design framework for pairing-based cryptography; a novel instruction scheduler eliminates pipeline conflicts, reaching 34x more throughput than a prior flexible design and 3x a fixed-function ASIC

groups.heading: Quantum computer control and compilation
groups.explain: A quantum chip is useless without a fast classical controller that generates precise microwave or laser pulses, reads back measurement results in microseconds, and feeds the results back into the next gate operation. Classical software running on a general-purpose CPU is too slow for this feedback loop — quantum states decay in microseconds. Beyond control electronics, quantum programs need compilers that reduce the number of physical operations before the quantum state degrades. The papers here span both: hardware that closes the classical feedback loop fast enough, and algorithms that shrink circuit size before execution.

papers.name: Distributed-HISQ
papers.gloss: Distributed control architecture where each controller pre-announces its sync points so others can prepare; eliminates round-trip wait time, cutting program execution time 22.8% and error rate 5x

papers.name: Qtenon
papers.gloss: RISC-V chip extended with quantum instructions and a shared memory buffer between classical and quantum processors; tight coupling cuts hybrid algorithm latency 14.9x over prior architectures

papers.name: ARTERY
papers.gloss: Applies branch prediction (predicting measurement outcomes before they arrive, like a CPU predicts branch directions) to quantum circuits; 2x lower feedback latency, 1.24x fidelity improvement
Calibration protocol for quantum processors that profiles each qubit pair individually and runs non-interfering calibrations in parallel; 8–25x less calibration time, 1.84x lower two-qubit gate error

papers.name: guoq
papers.gloss: Optimizer that alternates fast local rewrite rules with slower exhaustive resynthesis on promising subcircuits, achieving stronger gate-count reductions than either technique alone

papers.name: QuCLEAR
papers.gloss: Quantum compiler that moves all Clifford gates (a classically simulatable subset) to the end of the circuit and eliminates them via classical post-processing; up to 84% reduction in entangling gate depth

papers.name: HATT
papers.gloss: Builds the mapping from quantum chemistry problems to qubit operations in a way tailored to each molecule's specific structure; 5–25% fewer gates than generic mappings

papers.name: QR-Map
papers.gloss: Deterministic map-based circuit analysis that finds qubit reuse opportunities (measuring and resetting qubits mid-circuit) in polynomial time; 20% average qubit reduction, 25% depth reduction

papers.name: S-SYNC
papers.gloss: Compiler for trapped-ion quantum processors that optimizes qubit shuttling (physical movement) and SWAP gates jointly rather than sequentially; 3.69x fewer shuttle operations, 1.73x better success rate

papers.name: SwitchQNet
papers.gloss: Cross-layer compiler for quantum data centers that batches optical-switch reconfigurations across multiple communication operations to amortize setup cost; 8x latency reduction

papers.name: TQSim
papers.gloss: Noisy quantum circuit simulator that caches intermediate quantum states in a tree structure and reuses them across different noise trials; up to 3.89x faster simulation on HPC clusters

groups.heading: Quantum error correction hardware
groups.explain: Quantum information is fragile — stray electromagnetic fields flip qubits constantly. Quantum error correction (QEC) encodes one reliable 'logical qubit' in dozens or hundreds of physical qubits, running a continuous cycle of syndrome measurement (detecting errors without reading the data) and decoding (identifying what went wrong). The decoder must finish before the next error arrives — sub-microsecond on today's hardware — which rules out software running on a conventional CPU. These papers build purpose-built decoders and memory architectures that make fault-tolerant quantum computing physically realizable.

papers.name: Micro Blossom
papers.gloss: First hardware implementation of the exact blossom matching algorithm for quantum error decoding; one processing unit per qubit and per edge, running the hardest decoding step entirely in programmable logic at 0.8 microsecond average latency

papers.name: GLADIATOR
papers.gloss: Detects when a qubit has leaked into a higher energy level (a particularly damaging error type) using a 10-logic-gate lookup per qubit per cycle; 1.7–3.9x fewer cycles wasted on leakage correction, 16% lower logical error rate

papers.name: LSQCA
papers.gloss: Splits quantum memory into fast-access registers and a dense scan-access store; nearly doubles usable qubit count at only 5% execution time penalty by tolerating variable-latency qubit access

papers.name: HetEC
papers.gloss: Architecture that mixes two types of error-correcting codes — surface codes (easy to implement locally) and quantum LDPC codes (much more efficient at scale) — to get universal computation with better overall resource use

Constant-rate entanglement distillation protocol for quantum network links; converts noisy shared quantum states into reliable ones at a fixed fraction of the raw generation rate, unblocking distributed quantum computing

groups.heading: Photonic and analog computing for specific domains
groups.explain: Light travels through a waveguide at the speed of light and can perform matrix-vector multiplication optically — electrons push through a lens-shaped region and emerge weighted by the lens geometry, performing the multiply step of a dot product with near-zero energy. Analog chips (circuits where voltage levels encode numbers rather than binary 1s and 0s) similarly exploit physics to perform computation that would take many transistor operations digitally. These approaches trade programmability and precision for extreme energy efficiency in the domains where they apply.

papers.name: LightML
papers.gloss: First complete system-level photonic accelerator for ML including a matched memory and buffer design that keeps the optical core above 80% busy; delivers 325 trillion operations per second at 3 watts

papers.name: RLGS
papers.gloss: Reinforcement learning compiler that finds optimal sequences for generating entangled photon cluster states in photonic quantum computers; 31–58% less generation time, 38–58% fewer error-prone CZ gates

papers.name: Fat-Tree QRAM
papers.gloss: Quantum Random Access Memory that pipelines multiple simultaneous memory queries by duplicating router nodes in a fat-tree pattern; delivers constant memory bandwidth independent of memory size, vs shrinking bandwidth in prior designs

papers.name: DS-TPU
papers.gloss: Analog dynamical system chip that learns graph data directly on-device using feedback electric current as a loss signal; 810x faster than training on a GPU, at 5 watts, with 10.8% better accuracy than conventional graph neural networks

groups.heading: FPGAs and reconfigurable silicon as flexible accelerators
groups.explain: An FPGA (field-programmable gate array) is a chip whose internal wiring can be changed in software — not a fixed circuit but a reconfigurable one. This makes FPGAs attractive for workloads that evolve quickly or that need specialized data-path structure without the cost of a full custom chip. The challenge is that each FPGA model has a different internal structure, and connecting multiple FPGAs or sharing one FPGA among many users requires careful software abstractions. The papers here build those abstractions.

papers.name: RSN
papers.gloss: Treats the FPGA as a circuit-switched stream network rather than a sequential instruction processor; dynamically pipelines multiple neural-network layers simultaneously without re-programming the chip, matching GPU latency at 18% of the memory bandwidth

papers.name: Nyx
papers.gloss: FPGA virtualization system that adds virtual FIFO buffers between pipelined tasks so dependent stages can execute at different times on shared hardware; 1.26–8.87x throughput improvement over task-parallel FPGA sharing

papers.name: Harmonia
papers.gloss: Unified shell interface spec for cloud FPGAs that lets user accelerators run on different FPGA models without modification, hiding platform differences behind a standard port contract

papers.name: IDEA-GP
papers.gloss: FPGA accelerator for robotic mapping algorithms (SLAM, Structure from Motion) with a compiler that profiles the current task at runtime and dynamically schedules operators onto a shared PE array; 7.5–41.6x faster than CPU

groups.heading: Domain-specific silicon for robotics, rendering, and edge sensing
groups.explain: The final group covers workloads that are neither purely AI nor purely cryptographic, but that share the same root bottleneck: irregular memory access patterns and computation that alternates between dense and sparse phases. 3D scene reconstruction, robotic motion planning, and volumetric video streaming all require processing thousands of geometric primitives per frame, with the set of relevant primitives changing unpredictably. Purpose-built chips or chip extensions handle these patterns far more efficiently than general-purpose processors.

papers.name: RTGS
papers.gloss: Algorithm-hardware co-design for real-time 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM (simultaneous mapping and localization using cloud-like 3D scene representations); 48.8x faster than edge GPU, 82.5x more energy efficient

papers.name: REACT3D
papers.gloss: Edge ASIC for incremental training of 3D Gaussian scene models from live camera streams; predicts which scene elements need retraining via spatial coherence, skipping redundant work; 12x faster, 33x more energy efficient than Jetson AGX Orin

papers.name: GBU
papers.gloss: Plug-in rendering unit for edge GPUs that processes Gaussian scene elements row by row, sharing intermediate values between neighboring pixels and skipping Gaussians contributing less than a threshold; enables 60+ FPS AR/VR on Jetson hardware vs 7–17 FPS baseline

papers.name: Uni-Render
papers.gloss: Single reconfigurable ASIC that handles all major neural rendering algorithms (NeRF, 3D Gaussian Splatting, hybrid methods) by reconfiguring its internal dataflow at runtime; up to 119x faster than prior neural rendering hardware at 5 watts

GPU ray-tracing accelerator that keeps many more rays active simultaneously by freeing shader cores after they issue their ray query, then reusing cached geometry data across the larger in-flight ray set; 95% average speedup

papers.name: HiPER
papers.gloss: ASIC for robot navigation that interleaves neural-network inference with iterative model-predictive control optimization; a fractal interconnect and multi-level scheduler handle the alternating dense/sparse compute pattern; 10.75x faster than a gaming GPU

papers.name: Pirate
papers.gloss: VR streaming system that alternates which eye's view is transmitted, synthesizing the missing eye geometrically on-device using disparity maps; achieves 90 FPS at bandwidths as low as 0.1 bits per pixel
Total-cost model for computing satellites in low Earth orbit; shows that using high-efficiency AI chips (instead of commodity hardware) reduces total ownership cost 116x despite higher per-chip price

papers.name: SMX
papers.gloss: Heterogeneous chip pairing a new CPU instruction extension for irregular alignment cases with a 2D coprocessor for regular wavefront computation; covers DNA, protein, and text alignment in 0.34 mm2 of silicon, 256–744x faster than software

papers.name: BQSim
papers.gloss: GPU-accelerated quantum circuit simulator that batches many input states at once using decision diagrams to find shared subcomputations; 3.25x faster than cuQuantum, 311x faster than an open-source simulator

papers.name: VoLUT
papers.gloss: 3D volumetric video super-resolution system that pre-computes a neural network's outputs into a lookup table offline, then runs real-time upsampling on mobile phones using table lookups instead of neural network inference

papers.name: FedProphet
papers.gloss: Federated adversarial training system that splits a large model into sequential modules so memory-limited edge devices each train one slice; a server coordinator balances accuracy vs robustness dynamically

papers.name: RISSP
papers.gloss: Automated method to generate minimal RISC-V processors for flexible electronics (plastic-substrate chips) by selecting only the instructions an application actually uses; 40x more energy-efficient per instruction than a small standard RISC-V core

Encodes neural network weights as signal delay times and activations as signal arrival times rather than binary numbers; 11x better energy than spiking neural networks, 3.5x better than 8-bit digital arrays, while staying compatible with standard AI training software

Integrates a tensor-core-style matrix unit into an open-source RISC-V GPU; cooperative warp execution lets multiple threads share one tensor-core operation to reduce memory pressure; up to 3x utilization improvement

connect: Every paper in this theme is, at its core, fighting the same battle: the computation is cheap but moving the data to reach the computation is expensive, slow, or thermally ruinous. FHE chips embed arithmetic inside DRAM so ciphertext never crosses a bus; quantum control chips sit nanoseconds from the qubit to avoid latency in the feedback loop; edge rendering ASICs reuse cached Gaussian geometry across pixels to avoid redundant loads. The GPU's memory wall that throttles transformer inference is the same wall — just in a different domain — and the answer is always the same: shrink the distance between where data lives and where arithmetic happens.
